title: Russian grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Russian, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work; Russian's six cases arrive one at a time, each with the job it does. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is in Cyrillic with its stressed vowel marked (Russians don't write the mark; it's there to help you), and has a reading in Latin letters.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and what you are, and ask them the same: your first Russian conversation.
lessons.topic: Sentences without “am, is, are”; {{я|ya}} “I”, {{ты|ty}} and {{вы|vy}} “you”; {{Меня́ зову́т…|Menyá zovút…}}

goal.t: Здра́вствуйте! Меня́ зову́т А́нна. Я америка́нка.
goal.r: Zdrástvuyte! Menyá zovút Ánna. Ya amerikánka.
goal.tr: Hello! My name is Anna. I'm American.

dialog.tr: Nice to meet you. My name is Anna.

blocks.p: Look at what is missing in this conversation: Russian has no word for “am”, “is” or “are” in the present. {{Я студе́нт.|Ya studént.}} is, word for word, “I student”. There is no “a” or “the” either: Russian has no articles at all.

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{я|ya}} is “I”. “You” has two words. {{ты|ty}} is for one person you know well: a friend, a child, family. {{вы|vy}} is for someone you don't know well or who is older than you, and for more than one person. When in doubt, say {{вы|vy}}: Ivan and Anna have just met, so they say {{вы|vy}}. Hello works the same way: {{Здра́вствуйте!|Zdrástvuyte!}} to anyone, {{Приве́т!|Privét!}} “Hi!” to friends.

table: someone you don't know well, someone older, or more than one person

blocks.p: **Your name.** {{Меня́ зову́т…|Menyá zovút…}} “My name is…” is word for word “Me they call…”. Learn it as one block for now: a later lesson takes it apart. To ask, say {{Как вас зову́т?|Kak vas zovút?}} (polite) or {{Как тебя́ зову́т?|Kak tebyá zovút?}} (to a friend or a child).

**Men and women.** Words for people often have a form for a man and a form for a woman: {{студе́нт|studént}} / {{студе́нтка|studéntka}}, {{америка́нец|amerikánets}} / {{америка́нка|amerikánka}}, {{ру́сский|rússkiy}} / {{ру́сская|rússkaya}}. Anna says {{Я америка́нка|Ya amerikánka}}; a man says {{Я америка́нец|Ya amerikánets}}.

**Asking.** A yes-or-no question is the same sentence, with your voice going up on the word you're asking about: {{Вы студе́нт.|Vy studént.}} “You're a student.” → {{Вы студе́нт?|Vy studént?}} “Are you a student?”. And {{А вы?|A vy?}} or {{А ты?|A ty?}} “And you?” turns a question back to the other person.

ex.note: polite, or to more than one person
to a friend or a child
to a man you know well

blocks.means: the part of a word said louder and longer: in “banana”, the na in the middle.

blocks.tip: Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. Under every example there is a reading in Latin letters, and tapping an example lets you hear it. The mark over a vowel (á) shows the stress, which can fall anywhere in a Russian word. Russians don't write the mark: it is here to help you. The letter {{ё|yo}} (yo) is always stressed, so it never needs one.

mistakes.why: There is no “am” in the present: put {{я|ya}} and the word side by side.
To someone you don't know well, say {{вы|vy}}: {{Как вас зову́т?|Kak vas zovút?}}. {{Тебя́|Tebyá}} is for friends and children.

lessons.title: Ask “What's this?” and “Who's this?”
lessons.summary: Point at things and people, ask what and who they are, and say yes, no and not.
lessons.topic: {{э́то|éto}} “this is, it's”; {{что|shto}} and {{кто|kto}}; {{не|ne}} “not”; {{да|da}} and {{нет|net}}

goal.t: Что э́то? — Э́то борщ!
goal.r: Shto éto? — Éto borshch!
goal.tr: What's this? — It's borscht!

dialog.t: Нет, э́то не ма́ма. Э́то моя́ ба́бушка!
dialog.r: Net, éto ne máma. Éto moyá bábushka!
dialog.tr: No, that's not my mom. That's my grandma!

blocks.p: **{{Э́то|Éto}}.** {{Э́то|Éto}} means “this is”, “that is” or “it's”: one word, and no verb. Point and say {{Э́то чай.|Éto chay.}} “This is tea.” or {{Э́то А́нна.|Éto Ánna.}} “That's Anna.” Russian doesn't separate “this” and “that” here. ({{мой|moy}}, {{моя́|moyá}} and {{твоя́|tvoyá}} mean “my” and “your”: a lesson soon shows which is which.)

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a thing or an idea: brother, cat, tea, love.

blocks.p: **Who or what?** Ask {{Кто э́то?|Kto éto?}} about a person, and about an animal too, and {{Что э́то?|Shto éto?}} about a thing. Word for word: “Who this?”, “What this?”. The question word usually comes first, but {{А э́то кто?|A éto kto?}} “And who's this?” is fine too: {{а|a}} at the start means “and”, “and what about”.

**Yes, no and not.** {{да|da}} is “yes” and {{нет|net}} is “no”. To say “not”, put {{не|ne}} right before the word it denies: {{Э́то не чай.|Éto ne chay.}} “This isn't tea.” A full answer often has both: {{Нет, э́то не чай, э́то ко́фе.|Net, éto ne chay, éto kófe.}}

ex.tr: Is this water? — Yes, it's water.

blocks.tip: Listen to {{Москва́|Moskvá}} and {{молоко́|molokó}} “milk”: an o without the stress sounds like a. {{молоко́|molokó}} is said “malakó”. The reading keeps the spelling; the stress mark shows you which o stays an o.

mistakes.why: {{Э́то|Éto}} already means “this is”: no other word is needed.
For a person, ask {{кто|kto}} “who”; {{что|shto}} is for things.
“Not” before a word is {{не|ne}}. {{нет|net}} is “no”, an answer on its own.

practice.q: You point at a dog and ask what it is. You say…

lines.tr: No, that's not a pirozhok, it's a pancake!

lessons.title: Ask for what you want
lessons.summary: Order in a café and ask for things in a shop: “Can I have a coffee and some water, please?”
lessons.topic: {{хочу́|khochú}}, {{хоти́те|khotíte}} and {{Мо́жно…?|Mózhno…?}}; the thing you want: {{-а|-a}} becomes {{-у|-u}}

goal.t: Мо́жно ко́фе и во́ду, пожа́луйста?
goal.r: Mózhno kófe i vódu, pozháluysta?
goal.tr: Can I have a coffee and some water, please?

dialog.tr: I'd like a tea and a pizza.
Green, please. And can I have some water?

blocks.p: **Wanting.** {{Я хочу́…|Ya khochú…}} “I want…”, then the thing. A waiter asks {{Что вы хоти́те?|Shto vy khotíte?}} “What would you like?” ({{хоти́те|khotíte}} is the form for {{вы|vy}}; to a friend, {{хо́чешь|khóchesh'}}). {{Мо́жно…?|Mózhno…?}} “May I have…?” is softer: {{Мо́жно меню́?|Mózhno menyú?}} “Can I have the menu?”. Both are polite enough with {{пожа́луйста|pozháluysta}} “please”.

blocks.means: the last letter or letters of a word, which change to show what the word is doing in the sentence: {{вода́|vodá}} becomes {{во́ду|vódu}}.

blocks.p: **The thing you want changes its ending.** Look: {{вода́|vodá}} is “water”, but you say {{Я хочу́ во́ду|Ya khochú vódu}}. Words that end in {{-а|-a}} change it to {{-у|-u}}, and words in {{-я|-ya}} change it to {{-ю|-yu}}. Most other words stay as they are: {{чай|chay}}, {{ко́фе|kófe}}, {{сок|sok}}, {{молоко́|molokó}}, {{меню́|menyú}}. Russian changes endings to show what a word is doing; this one marks the thing you want, take or do something to. Lesson 10 shows it in full.

ex.tr: Can I have the menu, please?
Can I have the check, please?

ex.note: word for word “Thanks, I don't want.”

blocks.tip: {{Пожа́луйста|Pozháluysta}} means both “please” and “you're welcome”: {{Спаси́бо!|Spasíbo!}} “Thank you!” — {{Пожа́луйста!|Pozháluysta!}} “You're welcome!”

mistakes.why: The thing you want: {{-а|-a}} becomes {{-у|-u}}.
Only words that end in {{-а|-a}} or {{-я|-ya}} change. {{ко́фе|kófe}}, {{чай|chay}}, {{сок|sok}} and {{молоко́|molokó}} stay as they are.

lessons.title: Ask where things are
lessons.summary: Ask where something is and answer “Here it is”: your first step into Russian's three genders.
lessons.topic: Gender from the ending: {{он|on}}, {{она́|oná}}, {{оно́|onó}}; {{мой|moy}}, {{моя́|moyá}}, {{моё|moyó}}; {{где|gde}} and {{вот|vot}}

goal.t: Где мой телефо́н? — Вот он!
goal.r: Gde moy telefón? — Vot on!
goal.tr: Where's my phone? — Here it is!

dialog.tr: Here it is. Is that everything?

blocks.p: Pasha says “it” three different ways: {{он|on}}, {{она́|oná}} and {{оно́|onó}}. Every Russian noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, things included, and “it” follows that: a phone is “he” ({{он|on}}), a bag is “she” ({{она́|oná}}), a coat is neither ({{оно́|onó}}).

blocks.means: the group a noun belongs to: masculine, feminine or neuter. In Russian every noun has one, things too, and the words around it change to match.

blocks.p: **You can see the gender at the end of the word.** The words that go with a noun show it too, like {{мой|moy}} / {{моя́|moyá}} / {{моё|moyó}} “my” and {{твой|tvoy}} / {{твоя́|tvoyá}} / {{твоё|tvoyó}} “your” (to a friend).

**Two things to watch.** Words that end in the soft sign {{ь|'}} can be either, so learn them with their gender: {{день|den'}} “day” is masculine, {{дверь|dver'}} “door” is feminine. And a word for a man is masculine even when it ends in {{-а|-a}}: {{мой па́па|moy pápa}} “my dad”, {{мой дя́дя|moy dyádya}} “my uncle”.

**Where? Here!** {{Где…?|Gde…?}} “Where is…?” needs no verb. {{Вот|Vot}} means “here is” or “there is” when you point at something or hand it over: {{Вот он.|Vot on.}} “Here it is.”, {{Вот мой па́спорт.|Vot moy pásport.}} “Here's my passport.”

ex.tr: Where's my bag? — Here it is.
Where's your mom? — She's at home.
Where's the subway? — There it is.

ex.note: in writing, a dash often stands where English has “is” between two nouns

mistakes.why: {{телефо́н|telefón}} ends in a consonant, so it is masculine: {{мой|moy}}.

mistakes.tr: Where's my bag? — Here it is.
mistakes.why: “It” follows the gender: {{су́мка|súmka}} is feminine, so {{она́|oná}}.
A man is masculine whatever the ending: {{мой па́па|moy pápa}}.

lessons.title: Say what things are like
lessons.summary: Describe people, places and things: a big city, an interesting book, a new car.
lessons.topic: Adjectives agree with their noun: {{-ый|-yy}}, {{-ая|-aya}}, {{-ое|-oye}} (and {{-ий|-iy}}, {{-ой|-oy}}); {{како́й|kakóy}}?

goal.t: Москва́ — большо́й и краси́вый го́род.
goal.r: Moskvá — bol'shóy i krasívyy górod.
goal.tr: Moscow is a big, beautiful city.

dialog.t: Спаси́бо! Кварти́ра но́вая, а дом ста́рый.
dialog.r: Spasíbo! Kvartíra nóvaya, a dom stáryy.
dialog.tr: Thanks! The apartment is new, but the building is old.

dialog.t: Нет, ку́хня ма́ленькая, но о́чень удо́бная.
dialog.r: Net, kúkhnya málen'kaya, no óchen' udóbnaya.
dialog.tr: No, the kitchen is small, but very convenient.
And what's this? A new sofa?

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, new, red, interesting.

blocks.p: A Russian adjective takes the gender of its noun and shows it in its ending: {{но́вый дом|nóvyy dom}} “a new house”, {{но́вая кварти́ра|nóvaya kvartíra}} “a new apartment”, {{но́вое окно́|nóvoye oknó}} “a new window”. Dictionaries give the masculine form.

**Three small variations.** When the ending is stressed, masculine {{-ый|-yy}} becomes {{-ой|-oy}}: {{большо́й|bol'shóy}}, {{молодо́й|molodóy}} “young”. After {{к|k}}, {{г|g}}, {{х|kh}}, {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}} and {{щ|shch}}, Russian never writes {{ы|y}}, so {{-ий|-iy}}: {{ру́сский|rússkiy}}, {{хоро́ший|khoróshiy}}. And after {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}}, {{щ|shch}}, an unstressed {{-ое|-oye}} is written {{-ее|-eye}}: {{хоро́шее|khorósheye}}.

**Two places for an adjective.** Before the noun, it describes it: {{краси́вый го́род|krasívyy górod}} “a beautiful city”. After the noun, with nothing in between, it says what the noun is like: {{Го́род краси́вый.|Górod krasívyy.}} “The city is beautiful.” Still no “is”. To ask, use {{како́й|kakóy}}, which agrees too ({{како́й|kakóy}}, {{кака́я|kakáya}}, {{како́е|kakóye}}): {{Кака́я э́то маши́на?|Kakáya éto mashína?}} “What kind of car is it?”. It also means “what a…!”: {{Како́й краси́вый го́род!|Kakóy krasívyy górod!}}

ex.tr: This is a very interesting book.
Which car is it? — The red one.

ex.t: Мой брат высо́кий, а сестра́ ма́ленькая.
ex.r: Moy brat vysókiy, a sestrá málen'kaya.
ex.tr: My brother is tall, and my sister is little.
ex.note: {{а|a}} sets two things side by side: “and”, “while”

mistakes.why: {{маши́на|mashína}} is feminine ({{-а|-a}}), so the adjective is feminine too: {{но́вая|nóvaya}}.
After {{к|k}}, write {{и|i}}, never {{ы|y}}: {{ру́сский|rússkiy}}.

lessons.title: Talk about more than one
lessons.summary: Say “tickets”, “friends” and “my new sneakers”: Russian plurals and the words that go with them.
lessons.topic: Plurals in {{-ы|-y}}, {{-и|-i}}, {{-а|-a}}; {{они́|oní}}; {{мои́|moí}}, {{но́вые|nóvyye}}

goal.t: Э́то мои́ друзья́, Ма́ша и Ди́ма.
goal.r: Éto moí druz'yá, Másha i Díma.
goal.tr: These are my friends, Masha and Dima.

dialog.t: Мои́ ве́щи здесь: джи́нсы, ма́йки, кроссо́вки.
dialog.r: Moí véshchi zdes': dzhínsy, máyki, krossóvki.
dialog.tr: My things are here: jeans, T-shirts, sneakers.
The keys? Those are your keys, Mom!

blocks.means: the form of a word for more than one: book, books. The form for one is the singular.

blocks.p: Most Russian plurals end in {{-ы|-y}} or {{-и|-i}}. Masculine nouns add {{-ы|-y}}, and feminine nouns change {{-а|-a}} to {{-ы|-y}}: {{биле́т|bilét}} → {{биле́ты|biléty}}, {{ко́мната|kómnata}} → {{ко́мнаты|kómnaty}}. Neuter nouns end in {{-а|-a}} or {{-я|-ya}}: {{окно́|oknó}} → {{о́кна|ókna}}. The stress sometimes moves, so listen to each word.

**The spelling rule again.** After {{к|k}}, {{г|g}}, {{х|kh}}, {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}} and {{щ|shch}}, write {{и|i}}, not {{ы|y}}: {{кни́га|kníga}} → {{кни́ги|knígi}}, {{ключ|klyuch}} → {{ключи́|klyuchí}}, {{ма́йка|máyka}} → {{ма́йки|máyki}}. It's the same rule as in {{ру́сский|rússkiy}}.

**The words around it follow.** “They” is {{они́|oní}}, for any gender. In the plural there is one form for all three genders: {{мои́|moí}} “my”, {{твои́|tvoí}} “your”, {{но́вые|nóvyye}} “new” ({{-ие|-iye}} after the same seven letters: {{ру́сские|rússkiye}}, {{хоро́шие|khoróshiye}}), {{э́ти|éti}} “these”. But {{э́то|éto}} “this is, these are” never changes: {{Э́то мои́ друзья́.|Éto moí druz'yá.}}

**A few everyday words are irregular**: {{друг|drug}} → {{друзья́|druz'yá}} “friends”, {{брат|brat}} → {{бра́тья|brát'ya}}, {{челове́к|chelovék}} → {{лю́ди|lyúdi}} “people”, {{ребёнок|rebyónok}} → {{де́ти|déti}} “children”, {{го́род|górod}} → {{города́|gorodá}}, {{дом|dom}} → {{дома́|domá}}. Learn them as you meet them.

ex.tr: Where are my keys? — Here they are.
The people here are very kind.

mistakes.why: After {{г|g}}, write {{и|i}}: {{кни́ги|knígi}}.
“These are…” is still {{э́то|éto}}. {{э́ти|éti}} goes right before a noun: {{э́ти лю́ди|éti lyúdi}} “these people”.
The adjective follows its noun into the plural: {{ру́сские|rússkiye}}.

practice.tr: The new sneakers are very nice.

lessons.title: Say what you do
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing and what you do, and ask others: “I'm reading. And you?”
lessons.topic: Verbs in the present: the {{-ешь|-esh'}} pattern ({{рабо́тать|rabótat'}}, {{чита́ть|chitát'}}, {{знать|znat'}}, {{де́лать|délat'}})

goal.t: Что ты де́лаешь? — Я чита́ю.
goal.r: Shto ty délayesh'? — Ya chitáyu.
goal.tr: What are you doing? — I'm reading.

dialog.t: Я рабо́таю. А что ты чита́ешь?
dialog.r: Ya rabótayu. A shto ty chitáyesh'?
dialog.tr: I'm working. What are you reading?
A Russian novel. It's very interesting.

dialog.t: А Ма́ша и О́ля? Что они́ де́лают?
dialog.r: A Másha i Ólya? Shto oní délayut?
dialog.tr: And Masha and Olya? What are they doing?

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: work, read, know, be.
the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: “to work”. Russian infinitives usually end in {{-ть|-t'}}: {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}} “to work”.

blocks.p: Russian has one present tense for both “I read” and “I'm reading”: {{я чита́ю|ya chitáyu}}. What changes is the verb's ending, which shows who is doing it.

blocks.means: to change a verb's ending to match who does it: I work, she works.

blocks.p: **How to make the forms.** Take the infinitive, drop {{-ть|-t'}}, and add the ending for each person. Most verbs that end in {{-ать|-at'}} or {{-ять|-yat'}} work like this. The new words: {{мы|my}} “we”, and {{он|on}}, {{она́|oná}}, {{они́|oní}}, which you know.

**No “do”, no “am”.** A question is the same sentence with a rising voice: {{Ты зна́ешь?|Ty znáyesh'?}} “Do you know?”. “Not” is {{не|ne}} before the verb: {{Я не зна́ю.|Ya ne znáyu.}} “I don't know.” And since the ending already says who, Russians often drop the pronoun in a quick answer: {{Что де́лаешь? — Рабо́таю.|Shto délayesh'? — Rabótayu.}}

ex.tr: Do you know where the subway is?
What do you do in the evening?
ex.note: the same present for “do” and “are doing”

mistakes.why: {{чита́ть|chitát'}} is the dictionary form, “to read”. With {{я|ya}}, the verb ends in {{-ю|-yu}}.
{{-ешь|-esh'}} is for {{ты|ty}}; for {{он|on}} and {{она́|oná}} it's {{-ет|-et}}.
No “am” before a verb: {{я чита́ю|ya chitáyu}} is both “I read” and “I'm reading”.

practice.why: Russian has one present for both.

practice.q: A friend calls you. Choose your replies.

lines.r: Ya rabótayu. Ty znáyesh', gde Másha?
lines.tr: I'm working. Do you know where Masha is?

Your turn: what are you doing now, and what is someone near you doing? Use {{я|ya}} and {{он|on}}, {{она́|oná}} or {{они́|oní}}.

answers.r: Ya chitáyu, a moy brat slúshayet múzyku.

answers.r: Ya rabótayu, a moyá kóshka otdykháyet.

lessons.title: Say which languages you speak
lessons.summary: Say which languages you speak and how well, and what you like and watch.
lessons.topic: The {{-ишь|-ish'}} pattern ({{говори́ть|govorít'}}, {{смотре́ть|smotrét'}}, {{люби́ть|lyubít'}}); {{по-ру́сски|po-rússki}} and {{ру́сский язы́к|rússkiy yazýk}}

goal.t: Я немно́го говорю́ по-ру́сски.
goal.r: Ya nemnógo govoryú po-rússki.
goal.tr: I speak a little Russian.

dialog.t: Да, немно́го. Я понима́ю, но говорю́ ме́дленно.
dialog.r: Da, nemnógo. Ya ponimáyu, no govoryú médlenno.
dialog.tr: Yes, a little. I understand, but I speak slowly.
Thank you! And do you speak English?

dialog.t: Пло́хо. Но я ча́сто смотрю́ америка́нские фи́льмы.
dialog.r: Plókho. No ya chásto smotryú amerikánskiye fíl'my.
dialog.tr: Badly. But I often watch American movies.

blocks.p: Many verbs that end in {{-ить|-it'}}, and some in {{-еть|-et'}}, have {{и|i}} in their endings where {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}} has {{е|ye}}: {{ты говори́шь|ty govorísh'}}, {{он говори́т|on govorít}}. Their {{они́|oní}} form ends in {{-ят|-yat}} (or {{-ат|-at}}).

**Two patterns.** So Russian verbs follow one of two patterns: the {{-ешь|-esh'}} pattern of {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}} and the {{-ишь|-ish'}} pattern of {{говори́ть|govorít'}}. The {{ты|ty}} form tells you which, so learn it with the verb. Listen to the stress: in {{смотрю́|smotryú}} it's on the ending; in {{смо́тришь|smótrish'}} it moves back.

**An extra {{л|l}}.** When the part before the ending finishes in {{б|b}}, {{п|p}}, {{в|v}}, {{м|m}} or {{ф|f}}, the {{я|ya}} form adds {{л|l}}: {{люби́ть|lyubít'}} “to love, to like” → {{я люблю́|ya lyublyú}}, but {{ты лю́бишь|ty lyúbish'}}; {{гото́вить|gotóvit'}} “to cook” → {{я гото́влю|ya gotóvlyu}}. Only the {{я|ya}} form does this.

**Languages.** “Speak Russian” is {{говори́ть по-ру́сски|govorít' po-rússki}}: {{по-ру́сски|po-rússki}} means “in Russian”. With {{знать|znat'}} “know”, {{учи́ть|uchít'}} “learn” and {{люби́ть|lyubít'}}, use the language itself: {{ру́сский язы́к|rússkiy yazýk}} “the Russian language”. To say how well: {{хорошо́|khoroshó}} “well”, {{пло́хо|plókho}} “badly”, {{немно́го|nemnógo}} “a little”, {{ме́дленно|médlenno}} “slowly”, {{свобо́дно|svobódno}} “fluently”.

ex.tr: What are you watching? — A movie.

blocks.tip: Russian writes languages and nationalities with a small letter: {{ру́сский|rússkiy}}, {{англи́йский|anglíyskiy}}, {{америка́нец|amerikánets}}.

mistakes.why: With {{говори́ть|govorít'}}, say {{по-ру́сски|po-rússki}}. {{ру́сский язы́к|rússkiy yazýk}} goes with {{знать|znat'}}, {{учи́ть|uchít'}} and {{люби́ть|lyubít'}}.
{{люби́ть|lyubít'}} adds {{л|l}} in the {{я|ya}} form: {{люблю́|lyublyú}}.
{{говори́ть|govorít'}} follows the {{-ишь|-ish'}} pattern: {{говори́шь|govorísh'}}.

practice.q: How do you say “I speak Spanish”?
You're Mike, from New York, at a party in Moscow. Choose your replies.

lines.why: A man from America is {{америка́нец|amerikánets}}. {{америка́нский|amerikánskiy}} is an adjective: {{америка́нский фильм|amerikánskiy fil'm}}.

practice.tr: We understand, but we speak slowly.

practice.q: Say: “I don't understand. I speak a little Russian.”
practice.answer: Я не понима́ю. Я немно́го говорю́ по-ру́сски.
practice.r: Ya ne ponimáyu. Ya nemnógo govoryú po-rússki.

practice.q: Your turn: which languages do you speak, and how well? Use {{Я говорю́ по-…|Ya govoryú po-…}} with {{хорошо́|khoroshó}}, {{немно́го|nemnógo}} or {{свобо́дно|svobódno}}.

answers.t: Я свобо́дно говорю́ по-англи́йски и немно́го по-ру́сски.
answers.r: Ya svobódno govoryú po-anglíyski i nemnógo po-rússki.
answers.tr: I speak English fluently and a little Russian.

answers.t: Я говорю́ по-испа́нски, а сейча́с учу́ ру́сский язы́к.
answers.r: Ya govoryú po-ispánski, a seychás uchú rússkiy yazýk.
answers.tr: I speak Spanish, and now I'm learning Russian.

lessons.title: Say where you live and work
lessons.summary: Say where you live, work and study, and where people and things are: “I live in Moscow and work at a bank.”
lessons.topic: The prepositional case after {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} ({{где?|gde?}}); {{жить|zhit'}}: {{живу́|zhivú}}, {{живёшь|zhivyósh'}}

goal.t: Я живу́ в Москве́ и рабо́таю в ба́нке.
goal.r: Ya zhivú v Moskvé i rabótayu v bánke.
goal.tr: I live in Moscow and work at a bank.

dialog.t: Я рабо́таю в шко́ле. Я учи́тель.
dialog.r: Ya rabótayu v shkóle. Ya uchítel'.
dialog.tr: I work at a school. I'm a teacher.

dialog.t: А я рабо́таю на по́чте, в це́нтре.
dialog.r: A ya rabótayu na póchte, v tséntre.
dialog.tr: And I work at the post office, downtown.

blocks.p: Look at the places in this conversation: {{Петербу́рг|Peterbúrg}} becomes {{в Петербу́рге|v Peterbúrge}}, {{шко́ла|shkóla}} becomes {{в шко́ле|v shkóle}}. After {{в|v}} “in” and {{на|na}} “on, at”, a word saying where something is takes a new ending.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun that shows place, time or direction: in, on, at, to, from.
the form a noun takes to show its job in the sentence. Russian has six cases, each with its own endings. The dictionary form is one of them.
the case for where something is, after {{в|v}} and {{на|na}}, and for what you talk about, after {{о|o}}. It's never used without a preposition, hence the name.

blocks.p: **The ending is almost always {{-е|-e}}.** Words in {{-ия|-iya}} and feminine words in {{-ь|-'}} take {{-и|-i}}.

**{{в|v}} or {{на|na}}?** {{в|v}} is “in”, inside a place: {{в Москве́|v Moskvé}}, {{в ба́нке|v bánke}}, {{в па́рке|v párke}}, {{в шко́ле|v shkóle}}. {{на|na}} is “on”, and “at” for events, open spaces and some places you just learn: {{на рабо́те|na rabóte}} “at work”, {{на по́чте|na póchte}} “at the post office”, {{на у́лице|na úlitse}} “outside, on the street”, {{на конце́рте|na kontsérte}} “at a concert”, {{на мо́ре|na móre}} “at the seaside”. Foreign words ending in a vowel never change: {{в кафе́|v kafé}}, {{в метро́|v metró}}, {{в кино́|v kinó}} “at the movies”.

**Living.** {{жить|zhit'}} “to live” is a little irregular: {{я живу́|ya zhivú}}, {{ты живёшь|ty zhivyósh'}}, {{он живёт|on zhivyót}}, {{мы живём|my zhivyóm}}, {{вы живёте|vy zhivyóte}}, {{они́ живу́т|oní zhivút}}. And “at home” is one special word: {{до́ма|dóma}}.

ex.t: Па́па на рабо́те, а ма́ма до́ма.
ex.r: Pápa na rabóte, a máma dóma.
ex.tr: Dad's at work, and Mom's at home.
Where do you work? — In a store.
In summer we live at the dacha.
ex.note: a {{да́ча|dácha}} is a summer house outside the city

ex.tr: The book is on the table.
I'm at a café right now.

mistakes.why: After {{в|v}} saying where: {{-а|-a}} → {{-е|-e}}.
“At work” is {{на рабо́те|na rabóte}}: some places take {{на|na}}, and you learn them as you go.
Words in {{-ия|-iya}} end in {{-ии|-ii}}: {{в Росси́и|v Rossíi}}, {{в А́нглии|v Ánglii}}.

practice.q: A new neighbor asks about you. Choose your replies.
Ask a friend: “Where do you work?”
Your turn: where do you live, and where do you work or study? Start with {{Я живу́ в…|Ya zhivú v…}}

answers.r: Ya zhivú v Bóstone i rabótayu v bol'nítse.
answers.tr: I live in Boston and work at a hospital.

lessons.title: Say what you like and what you're doing
lessons.summary: Talk about what you love, read, watch and cook: the form a noun takes when something is done to it.
lessons.topic: The accusative case of things: {{-у|-u}}, {{-ю|-yu}}, adjectives {{-ую|-uyu}}; {{люблю́|lyublyú}} + infinitive

goal.t: Я о́чень люблю́ ру́сскую му́зыку.
goal.r: Ya óchen' lyublyú rússkuyu múzyku.
goal.tr: I really love Russian music.

dialog.t: Что ты лю́бишь де́лать в свобо́дное вре́мя?
dialog.r: Shto ty lyúbish' délat' v svobódnoye vrémya?
dialog.tr: What do you like to do in your free time?

dialog.t: Я люблю́ гото́вить. И я люблю́ смотре́ть фи́льмы.
dialog.r: Ya lyublyú gotóvit'. I ya lyublyú smotrét' fíl'my.
dialog.tr: I like to cook. And I like watching movies.
What kind of movies do you like?

dialog.t: А я люблю́ му́зыку. Я игра́ю на гита́ре.
dialog.r: A ya lyublyú múzyku. Ya igráyu na gitáre.
dialog.tr: And I love music. I play the guitar.

blocks.means: the person or thing doing the action: in “Anna reads a book”, Anna.
the person or thing the action is done to: in “Anna reads a book”, a book.

blocks.p: In English, the order of the words shows who does what: “Anna reads the book”. In Russian, the endings show it. The subject stays in the dictionary form, and the object takes the **accusative**: {{кни́га|kníga}} becomes {{кни́гу|knígu}} in {{А́нна чита́ет кни́гу|Ánna chitáyet knígu}}. You've used it since lesson 3: {{Я хочу́ во́ду.|Ya khochú vódu.}}

blocks.means: the dictionary form of a noun, used for the subject: {{кни́га|kníga}}, {{Москва́|Moskvá}}.
the case of the object, the thing you read, want, love or do something to: {{Я чита́ю кни́гу.|Ya chitáyu knígu.}}

blocks.p: So for things, only feminine words in {{-а|-a}} and {{-я|-ya}} change. An adjective with them changes too, {{-ая|-aya}} → {{-ую|-uyu}}: {{Я люблю́ ру́сскую ку́хню.|Ya lyublyú rússkuyu kúkhnyu.}} “I love Russian food.” ({{ку́хня|kúkhnya}} means both “kitchen” and “cuisine”.)

**Love to do.** {{люби́ть|lyubít'}} works with a noun or with another verb in the infinitive: {{Я люблю́ гото́вить.|Ya lyublyú gotóvit'.}} “I like to cook.” Russians use it for things they like a lot, not only for people.

ex.t: Я люблю́ гуля́ть и слу́шать му́зыку.
ex.r: Ya lyublyú gulyát' i slúshat' múzyku.
ex.tr: I like going for walks and listening to music.

mistakes.why: The object: {{-а|-a}} → {{-у|-u}}, and its adjective {{-ая|-aya}} → {{-ую|-uyu}}.
After {{люблю́|lyublyú}}, the second verb stays in the infinitive, in {{-ть|-t'}}.

practice.q: In {{Я смотрю́ фильм|Ya smotryú fil'm}}, why doesn't {{фильм|fil'm}} change?
options: Masculine things don't change in the accusative.
practice.why: Only feminine words in {{-а|-a}} and {{-я|-ya}} change when they're things.

practice.tr: I like to cook and watch movies.

And what are you reading now?

practice.r: Ya zhivú v Moskvé i lyublyú rússkuyu múzyku.

practice.q: Your turn: what do you like doing, and what are you reading or watching right now? Use {{Я люблю́…|Ya lyublyú…}} and {{Сейча́с я чита́ю / смотрю́…|Seychás ya chitáyu / smotryú…}}

answers.t: Я люблю́ гото́вить. Сейча́с я чита́ю интере́сную кни́гу.
answers.r: Ya lyublyú gotóvit'. Seychás ya chitáyu interésnuyu knígu.
answers.tr: I like to cook. Right now I'm reading an interesting book.

lessons.title: Talk about people you know
lessons.summary: Say whom you know, love, see and wait for, and find out at last how {{Меня́ зову́т|Menyá zovút}} works.
lessons.topic: The accusative of people: {{бра́та|bráta}}, {{А́нну|Ánnu}}; {{меня́|menyá}}, {{тебя́|tebyá}}, {{его́|yevó}}, {{её|yeyó}}, {{нас|nas}}, {{вас|vas}}, {{их|ikh}}

goal.t: Ты зна́ешь Ива́на? — Да, я его́ хорошо́ зна́ю.
goal.r: Ty znáyesh' Ivána? — Da, ya yevó khoroshó znáyu.
goal.tr: Do you know Ivan? — Yes, I know him well.

dialog.tr: Lena? Of course I know her.

dialog.t: Макси́ма? Нет, я его́ не зна́ю.
dialog.r: Maksíma? Net, ya yevó ne znáyu.
dialog.tr: Maxim? No, I don't know him.

dialog.t: Он о́чень симпати́чный. Я его́ жду.
dialog.r: On óchen' simpatíchnyy. Ya yevó zhdu.
dialog.tr: He's really nice. I'm waiting for him.

blocks.p: In the last lesson, masculine things didn't change in the accusative: {{Я смотрю́ фильм.|Ya smotryú fil'm.}} Masculine **people and animals** do: they add {{-а|-a}} (or {{-я|-ya}}): {{Я зна́ю Ива́на.|Ya znáyu Ivána.}} {{Я жду бра́та.|Ya zhdu bráta.}} {{Я люблю́ кота́.|Ya lyublyú kotá.}} Women change like feminine things: {{А́нна|Ánna}} → {{А́нну|Ánnu}}, {{ма́ма|máma}} → {{ма́му|mámu}}. Words with them change too: {{мой брат|moy brat}} → {{моего́ бра́та|moyevó bráta}}, {{но́вый друг|nóvyy drug}} → {{но́вого дру́га|nóvovo drúga}} (the {{г|g}} in {{-ого|-ogo}} is said v).

table: a man or a male animal

blocks.p: **Me, him, her.** Pronouns have their own accusative, and it usually comes before the verb: {{Я его́ зна́ю.|Ya yevó znáyu.}} “I know him.”

**Now you can read {{Меня́ зову́т|Menyá zovút}}.** {{зову́т|zovút}} is “(they) call”, and {{меня́|menyá}} is “me”: “they call me Anna”. So you ask {{Как тебя́ зову́т?|Kak tebyá zovút?}}, and about others {{Как его́ зову́т?|Kak yevó zovút?}} “What's his name?”, {{Как её зову́т?|Kak yeyó zovút?}} “What's her name?”.

ex.tr: I love my mom and dad.
ex.note: Russian leaves out “my” when it's obvious

ex.t: Ты ви́дишь Ди́му? — Да, я его́ ви́жу.
ex.r: Ty vídish' Dímu? — Da, ya yevó vízhu.
ex.tr: Do you see Dima? — Yes, I see him.

ex.note: {{ждать|zhdat'}} “wait for” takes the accusative, with no word for “for”

ex.t: Как её зову́т? — Её зову́т Ка́тя.
ex.r: Kak yeyó zovút? — Yeyó zovút Kátya.
ex.tr: What's her name? — Her name is Katya.

mistakes.why: A man as the object: add {{-а|-a}}.
“Him” is {{его́|yevó}} (said “yevó”), usually before the verb.
“Wait for” is just {{ждать|zhdat'}} and the accusative.

practice.q: How do you ask “What's his name?”
At work, a colleague asks you about people. Choose your replies.

options: Нет, я не зна́ю его́ муж.
lines.why: “Him”: {{его́|yevó}}. (A man as the object would be {{му́жа|múzha}}.)

lines.t: Вот он! Пойдём, я вас познако́млю.
lines.r: Vot on! Poydyóm, ya vas poznakómlyu.

practice.q: Your turn: name two people you know or love, and say what they're called. Use {{Я люблю́…|Ya lyublyú…}} or {{Я зна́ю…|Ya znáyu…}}, and {{Его́ / Её зову́т…|Yevó / Yeyó zovút…}}

answers.t: Я о́чень люблю́ ба́бушку. Её зову́т Мэ́ри.
answers.r: Ya óchen' lyublyú bábushku. Yeyó zovút Méri.

answers.t: Я хорошо́ зна́ю сосе́да. Его́ зову́т Боб.

answers.tr: I know my neighbor well. His name is Bob.

lessons.title: Say what you did yesterday
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did and where you were: the Russian past, which follows the speaker's gender.
lessons.topic: The past tense: {{-л|-l}}, {{-ла|-la}}, {{-ло|-lo}}, {{-ли|-li}}; {{был|byl}}, {{была́|bylá}}, {{бы́ли|býli}}

goal.t: Вчера́ я была́ до́ма и смотре́ла фильм.
goal.r: Vcherá ya bylá dóma i smotréla fil'm.
goal.tr: Yesterday I was at home and watched a movie.
goal.note: said by a woman; a man says {{был|byl}} and {{смотре́л|smotrél}}

dialog.tr: Hi! What did you do yesterday?

dialog.t: Я была́ на конце́рте. А ты?
dialog.r: Ya bylá na kontsérte. A ty?
dialog.tr: I was at a concert. And you?

dialog.t: А я был до́ма. Я рабо́тал.
dialog.r: A ya byl dóma. Ya rabótal.
dialog.tr: I was at home. I worked.

dialog.t: Нет, ве́чером мы гуля́ли в па́рке.
dialog.r: Net, vécherom my gulyáli v párke.
dialog.tr: No, in the evening we went for a walk in the park.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: present (I work), past (I worked), future (I will work).

blocks.p: The Russian past is easy to make: take the infinitive, drop {{-ть|-t'}}, and add {{-л|-l}}. But it doesn't change for “I, you, he” like the present. It changes for **gender**, like an adjective: {{-л|-l}} for a man, {{-ла|-la}} for a woman, {{-ло|-lo}} for an “it”, {{-ли|-li}} for more than one, and always with {{вы|vy}}.

**So “I” has two pasts.** A man says {{я был|ya byl}}, a woman {{я была́|ya bylá}}. Talking to someone, you choose by them: {{Где ты был?|Gde ty byl?}} to a man, {{Где ты была́?|Gde ty bylá?}} to a woman.

**The past has “was”.** The present has no “is”, but the past does: {{Я до́ма.|Ya dóma.}} “I'm at home.” → {{Я был до́ма.|Ya byl dóma.}} “I was at home.” With {{не|ne}}, the stress jumps onto it: {{я не́ был|ya né byl}}, {{мы не́ были|my né byli}} (but {{она́ не была́|oná ne bylá}}).

ex.t: Где ты была́? — Я была́ в магази́не.
ex.r: Gde ty bylá? — Ya bylá v magazíne.
ex.tr: Where were you? — I was at the store.
ex.note: to a woman, and her answer

ex.tr: They used to live in Kazan.
What did you do last night?

ex.note: a man; the stress moves to {{не|ne}}

mistakes.tr: I was at home. (a woman speaking)
mistakes.why: A woman says {{я была́|ya bylá}}: the past follows the speaker's gender.
Yesterday is the past: {{-л|-l}}.
With {{мы|my}}, {{вы|vy}} and {{они́|oní}}, the past ends in {{-ли|-li}}.

practice.tr: Yesterday Anna was at the theater.

practice.q: A man asks a woman “Where were you?”. He says…
practice.why: The verb follows the person it's about: she's a woman.

practice.q: You're a man. A friend calls you. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: And what did you do in the evening?

practice.q: Say, as a woman: “Yesterday I saw Ivan.”
Your turn: what did you do yesterday? Say where you were and two things you did.

answers.t: Вчера́ я был на рабо́те, а ве́чером смотре́л фильм.
answers.r: Vcherá ya byl na rabóte, a vécherom smotrél fil'm.
answers.tr: Yesterday I was at work, and in the evening I watched a movie.

answers.r: Vcherá ya bylá dóma. Ya chitála i gotóvila úzhin.
answers.tr: Yesterday I was at home. I read and made dinner.

lessons.title: Say what you have
lessons.summary: Say what you have, and ask in shops and hotels: “Do you have a room for tonight?”
lessons.topic: {{У меня́ есть|U menyá yest'}}; {{у тебя́|u tebyá}}, {{у него́|u nevó}}, {{у неё|u neyó}}… (with {{н|n}} after {{у|u}})

goal.t: У вас есть свобо́дный но́мер? — Да, есть.
goal.r: U vas yest' svobódnyy nómer? — Da, yest'.
goal.tr: Do you have a room available? — Yes, we do.

dialog.t: Спаси́бо. У меня́ то́лько ка́рта. Мо́жно ка́ртой?
dialog.r: Spasíbo. U menyá tól'ko kárta. Mózhno kártoy?
dialog.tr: Thank you. I only have a card. Can I pay by card?

blocks.p: Russian has a verb for “to have”, but in everyday speech nobody uses it for owning things. Instead, Russians say {{У меня́ есть…|U menyá yest'…}}, word for word “At me there is…”. What you have is the subject, so it stays in the nominative: {{У меня́ есть маши́на.|U menyá yest' mashína.}} “I have a car.”

table: {{У меня́ есть вре́мя.|U menyá yest' vrémya.}}
{{У тебя́ есть ру́чка?|U tebyá yest' rúchka?}}
{{У него́ есть соба́ка.|U nevó yest' sobáka.}}
{{У неё есть маши́на.|U neyó yest' mashína.}}
{{У нас есть да́ча.|U nas yest' dácha.}}
{{У вас есть меню́?|U vas yest' menyú?}}
{{У них есть де́ти.|U nikh yest' déti.}}

blocks.p: **An extra {{н|n}}.** After {{у|u}}, and after most other prepositions, “him”, “her” and “them” start with {{н|n}}: {{у него́|u nevó}}, {{у неё|u neyó}}, {{у них|u nikh}}. Without a preposition, {{его́|yevó}}, {{её|yeyó}} and {{их|ikh}} mean “his”, “her” and “their”: {{у него́ есть маши́на|u nevó yest' mashína}} “he has a car”, {{его́ маши́на|yevó mashína}} “his car”.

**Asking and answering.** {{У вас есть…?|U vas yest'…?}} is how you ask in shops, hotels and cafés: “Do you have…?”. The short answer is {{Есть.|Yest'.}} or {{Да, есть.|Da, yest'.}} When what matters isn't whether you have it but what it's like, leave out {{есть|yest'}}: {{У неё больша́я семья́.|U neyó bol'sháya sem'yá.}} “She has a big family.”

ex.t: У тебя́ есть ру́чка? — Да, вот она́.
ex.r: U tebyá yest' rúchka? — Da, vot oná.
ex.tr: Do you have a pen? — Yes, here it is.

ex.t: У нас есть ко́шка и соба́ка.
ex.r: U nas yest' kóshka i sobáka.
ex.tr: We have a cat and a dog.

ex.note: no {{есть|yest'}}: what matters is that it's new

blocks.tip: In the past, {{есть|yest'}} becomes {{был|byl}}, {{была́|bylá}}, {{бы́ло|býlo}} or {{бы́ли|býli}}, agreeing with the thing you had: {{У меня́ была́ маши́на.|U menyá bylá mashína.}} “I had a car.”

mistakes.why: In everyday Russian, “I have” is {{у меня́ есть|u menyá yest'}}, and the thing is in the nominative.
After {{у|u}}: {{него́|nevó}}, with {{н|n}}.
What you have is the subject: the nominative {{маши́на|mashína}}.

practice.q: {{У меня́ есть|U menyá yest'}} is, word for word…
practice.why: The owner comes after {{у|u}} “at”, and the thing is the subject.

practice.q: At a hotel: choose your replies.

options: Здра́вствуйте! У вас есть свобо́дный но́мер?
lines.why: Ask with {{У вас есть…?|U vas yest'…?}}

options: Да. А за́втрак у вас есть?
Да. А за́втрака у вас есть?
lines.why: With {{есть|yest'}}, the thing stays in the nominative: {{за́втрак|závtrak}}.

answers.r: U menyá yest' kot i velosipéd. A u tebyá yest' sobáka?
answers.tr: I have a cat and a bike. Do you have a dog?

answers.r: U menyá yest' mashína. U tebyá yest' vrémya závtra?
answers.tr: I have a car. Do you have time tomorrow?

lessons.title: Say what you don't have, and what isn't there
lessons.summary: Say you don't have something, that something isn't there, or that someone isn't in: “Sorry, I don't have time.”
lessons.topic: {{нет|net}} and the genitive case: {{-а|-a}}, {{-я|-ya}}, {{-ы|-y}}, {{-и|-i}}; {{у бра́та|u bráta}}

goal.t: Извини́те, у меня́ нет вре́мени.
goal.r: Izviníte, u menyá net vrémeni.
goal.tr: Sorry, I don't have time.

dialog.tr: Hello! May I speak to Ivan Petrovich?

dialog.t: На встре́че. А у вас есть его́ но́мер?
dialog.r: Na vstréche. A u vas yest' yevó nómer?
dialog.tr: In a meeting. Do you have his number?

dialog.t: Нет, у меня́ нет его́ но́мера.
dialog.r: Net, u menyá net yevó nómera.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have his number.

blocks.p: {{нет|net}} isn't only “no”. It also means “there isn't, there's no”: {{Здесь нет ба́нка.|Zdes' net bánka.}} “There's no bank here.” And the thing that isn't there takes a new case, the **genitive**: {{банк|bank}} → {{ба́нка|bánka}}.

blocks.means: the case for what isn't there ({{нет вре́мени|net vrémeni}} “no time”), for “of” ({{ча́шка ча́я|cháshka cháya}} “a cup of tea”), for amounts and for “from”. After {{у|u}} it names the owner.

blocks.p: **I don't have.** {{У меня́ есть|U menyá yest'}} becomes {{У меня́ нет|U menyá net}} and the genitive: {{У меня́ нет маши́ны.|U menyá net mashíny.}} “I don't have a car.” The everyday word {{вре́мя|vrémya}} “time” is irregular: {{нет вре́мени|net vrémeni}}.

**Someone isn't here.** For a person, it's {{нет|net}} and the person in the genitive: {{Его́ нет.|Yevó net.}} “He isn't here, he isn't in.” {{Ма́мы нет до́ма.|Mámy net dóma.}} “Mom isn't home.” The pronouns look like the accusative ones: {{меня́|menyá}}, {{тебя́|tebyá}}, {{его́|yevó}}, {{её|yeyó}}, {{нас|nas}}, {{вас|vas}}, {{их|ikh}}.

**Who has it.** The same genitive comes after {{у|u}} with nouns and names: {{У бра́та есть маши́на.|U bráta yest' mashína.}} “My brother has a car.” {{У А́нны нет вре́мени.|U Ánny net vrémeni.}} “Anna has no time.”

ex.t: У меня́ нет бра́та, но есть сестра́.
ex.r: U menyá net bráta, no yest' sestrá.
ex.tr: I don't have a brother, but I have a sister.
There's no milk in the fridge.

blocks.tip: In the past, {{нет|net}} becomes {{не́ было|né bylo}}, whatever the thing: {{Вчера́ у меня́ не́ было вре́мени.|Vcherá u menyá né bylo vrémeni.}} “Yesterday I had no time.”

mistakes.why: After {{нет|net}}: the genitive.
“There isn't” is one word: {{нет|net}}.
Someone who isn't there is in the genitive after {{нет|net}}: {{его́|yevó}}, {{А́нны|Ánny}}.

practice.q: How do you say “He isn't home”?
options: {{У него́ нет до́ма.|U nevó net dóma.}}
practice.why: {{Его́ нет до́ма|Yevó net dóma}}: he isn't at home. {{У него́ нет до́ма|U nevó net dóma}} would mean he has no house!

practice.q: In a small shop: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{есть|yest'}} takes the nominative; {{нет|net}} takes the genitive.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you don't have, or what there isn't in your town, and what there is instead. Use {{У меня́ нет…|U menyá net…}} or {{Здесь нет…|Zdes' net…}}, then {{но есть…|no yest'…}}

answers.t: У меня́ нет маши́ны, но есть велосипе́д.
answers.r: U menyá net mashíny, no yest' velosipéd.
answers.tr: I don't have a car, but I have a bike.

answers.t: Здесь нет метро́, но есть большо́й парк.
answers.r: Zdes' net metró, no yest' bol'shóy park.
answers.tr: There's no subway here, but there's a big park.

lessons.title: Ask what things cost
lessons.summary: Count, ask “How much is it?” and understand prices: one ruble, two rubles, five rubles.
lessons.topic: Numbers; {{Ско́лько сто́ит?|Skól'ko stóit?}}; {{рубль|rubl'}}, {{рубля́|rublyá}}, {{рубле́й|rubléy}} after 1, 2–4 and 5+

goal.t: Ско́лько сто́ит э́та футбо́лка? — Пятьсо́т рубле́й.
goal.r: Skól'ko stóit éta futbólka? — Pyat'sót rubléy.
goal.tr: How much is this T-shirt? — Five hundred rubles.

dialog.tr: A hundred and twenty rubles a kilo.
That's a hundred and twenty rubles.

blocks.p: **Numbers.** Learn 1 to 10 first; the rest are built from them.

Bigger numbers are put side by side: {{два́дцать оди́н|dvádtsat' odín}} (21), {{сто пятьдеся́т|sto pyat'desyát}} (150), {{ты́сяча две́сти|týsyacha dvésti}} (1,200). From 11 to 19 they end in {{-на́дцать|-nádtsat'}}: {{оди́ннадцать|odínnadtsat'}}, {{двена́дцать|dvenádtsat'}}, {{пятна́дцать|pyatnádtsat'}}. One and two agree with their noun: {{оди́н рубль|odín rubl'}} but {{одна́ ты́сяча|odná týsyacha}}; {{два рубля́|dva rublyá}} but {{две ты́сячи|dve týsyachi}}.

**How much?** {{Ско́лько сто́ит…?|Skól'ko stóit…?}} “How much does … cost?” for one thing, {{Ско́лько сто́ят…?|Skól'ko stóyat…?}} for several. To point at it, {{э́тот|étot}}, {{э́та|éta}}, {{э́то|éto}}, {{э́ти|éti}} “this, these” agree like adjectives: {{э́та футбо́лка|éta futbólka}}, {{э́ти я́блоки|éti yábloki}}.

**The noun after a number.** Here is a Russian surprise: the noun changes with the number. After 1 (and 21, 31…): the nominative, {{оди́н рубль|odín rubl'}}. After 2, 3, 4 (and 22, 33…): the genitive singular you met with {{нет|net}}, {{два рубля́|dva rublyá}}. After 5 to 20, and after round tens and hundreds: the genitive plural, {{пять рубле́й|pyat' rubléy}}. For now, learn the three forms of the words you need most; a later lesson shows how to make them.

ex.tr: How much is a ticket? — Three hundred rubles.
The coffee is a hundred and fifty rubles.

mistakes.why: From 5 up: {{рубле́й|rubléy}}. {{рубля́|rublyá}} is for 2, 3 and 4.
Several things: {{сто́ят|stóyat}}.
{{ты́сяча|týsyacha}} is feminine: {{две|dve}}.

practice.tr: The ticket costs five hundred rubles.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.

lines.why: What you ask for is in the accusative: masculine {{килогра́мм|kilográmm}} doesn't change.

lines.tr: Here you go. That's two hundred rubles.

answers.r: Skól'ko stóit éta súmka? Tri týsyachi? Éto dórogo!
answers.tr: How much is this bag? Three thousand? That's expensive!

answers.t: Ско́лько сто́ят биле́ты? Пятьсо́т рубле́й? Э́то недо́рого.
answers.r: Skól'ko stóyat biléty? Pyat'sót rubléy? Éto nedórogo.

lessons.title: Talk about your family and your age
lessons.summary: Say who's in your family and how old everyone is, and ask about someone else's family.
lessons.topic: {{Мне два́дцать лет|Mne dvádtsat' let}}: {{мне|mne}}, {{тебе́|tebé}}, {{ему́|yemú}}, {{ей|yey}}… as set phrases; {{год|god}}, {{го́да|góda}}, {{лет|let}}

goal.t: Мне три́дцать лет. У меня́ есть брат и сестра́.
goal.r: Mne trídtsat' let. U menyá yest' brat i sestrá.
goal.tr: I'm thirty. I have a brother and a sister.

dialog.tr: Do you have a big family?

dialog.t: Нет, ма́ленькая. У меня́ есть ста́рший брат.
dialog.r: Net, málen'kaya. U menyá yest' stárshiy brat.
dialog.tr: No, a small one. I have an older brother.

dialog.t: Ему́ три́дцать два го́да. А тебе́ ско́лько лет?
dialog.r: Yemú trídtsat' dva góda. A tebé skól'ko let?
dialog.tr: He's thirty-two. And how old are you?

dialog.t: Мне два́дцать пять. А у меня́ есть сестра́, ей де́сять лет.
dialog.r: Mne dvádtsat' pyat'. A u menyá yest' sestrá, yey désyat' let.
dialog.tr: I'm twenty-five. And I have a sister, she's ten.

blocks.p: To say your age, Russian says “To me thirty years”: {{Мне три́дцать лет.|Mne trídtsat' let.}} There's no “am”, and the person takes a new form, {{мне|mne}} “to me”. Learn these forms with the phrase for now: they belong to the dative case, which gets its own lesson later.

table: {{Нам по два́дцать лет.|Nam po dvádtsat' let.}}

blocks.p: **Year, years.** {{год|god}} follows the number rule from the last lesson, with one twist: after 5 it becomes a different word, {{лет|let}}. So: {{Мне два́дцать оди́н год.|Mne dvádtsat' odín god.}} {{Мне два́дцать два го́да.|Mne dvádtsat' dva góda.}} {{Мне два́дцать пять лет.|Mne dvádtsat' pyat' let.}} ({{Нам по два́дцать лет|Nam po dvádtsat' let}}: {{по|po}} means “each”.)

**Family.** {{ма́ма|máma}} and {{па́па|pápa}} (or, more formally, {{мать|mat'}} and {{оте́ц|otéts}}), {{роди́тели|rodíteli}} “parents”, {{брат|brat}}, {{сестра́|sestrá}}, {{сын|syn}} “son”, {{дочь|doch'}} “daughter”, {{де́ти|déti}} “children”, {{муж|muzh}} “husband”, {{жена́|zhená}} “wife”, {{ба́бушка|bábushka}} and {{де́душка|dédushka}}. Brothers and sisters can be {{ста́рший|stárshiy}} “older” or {{мла́дший|mládshiy}} “younger”.
**Someone else's family.** “His”, “her” and “their” are {{его́|yevó}}, {{её|yeyó}} and {{их|ikh}}, and they never change: {{его́ жена́|yevó zhená}}, {{её брат|yeyó brat}}, {{их де́ти|ikh déti}}.

ex.t: Ско́лько вам лет? — Мне со́рок оди́н год.
ex.r: Skól'ko vam let? — Mne sórok odín god.
ex.tr: How old are you? — I'm forty-one.

ex.t: У меня́ есть сын и дочь.
ex.r: U menyá yest' syn i doch'.
ex.tr: I have a son and a daughter.

ex.t: У него́ есть де́ти? — Да, два сы́на.
ex.r: U nevó yest' déti? — Da, dva sýna.
ex.tr: Does he have children? — Yes, two sons.
My younger brother is still a student.

mistakes.why: Age is {{мне|mne}} and the number: “to me thirty years”.
After 5 to 20 (and 25…): {{лет|let}}. {{го́да|góda}} goes after 2, 3, 4.
Ask “how many years to you”: {{Ско́лько тебе́ лет?|Skól'ko tebé let?}}

practice.q: How do you politely ask a new colleague how old they are?
A friend asks about your family. Choose your replies.

lines.t: У тебя́ есть бра́тья и́ли сёстры?
lines.r: U tebyá yest' brát'ya íli syóstry?
lines.tr: Do you have brothers or sisters?

answers.t: У меня́ есть брат. Его́ зову́т Том, ему́ два́дцать два го́да.
answers.r: U menyá yest' brat. Yevó zovút Tom, yemú dvádtsat' dva góda.
answers.tr: I have a brother. His name is Tom, he's twenty-two.

answers.r: U menyá yest' doch'. Yey pyat' let.

lessons.title: Say what time and which day
lessons.summary: Ask the time, say when things happen, and make plans for a day of the week: “On Saturday at seven.”
lessons.topic: {{Кото́рый час?|Kotóryy chas?}}; {{в|v}} + time ({{в два часа́|v dva chasá}}); {{в|v}} + day ({{в сре́ду|v srédu}}); {{у́тром|útrom}}, {{ве́чером|vécherom}}

goal.t: Конце́рт в суббо́ту в семь часо́в ве́чера.
goal.r: Kontsért v subbótu v sem' chasóv véchera.
goal.tr: The concert is on Saturday at seven in the evening.

dialog.tr: What are you doing on Saturday?

dialog.t: В суббо́ту конце́рт в па́рке. Хо́чешь?
dialog.r: V subbótu kontsért v párke. Khóchesh'?
dialog.tr: There's a concert in the park on Saturday. Want to come?

dialog.t: Отли́чно! Ой, а сейча́с кото́рый час? Я опа́здываю!
dialog.r: Otlíchno! Oy, a seychás kotóryy chas? Ya opázdyvayu!
dialog.tr: Great! Oh, what time is it now? I'm late!

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{Кото́рый час?|Kotóryy chas?}} or, more casually, {{Ско́лько вре́мени?|Skól'ko vrémeni?}}. The answer is a number with {{час|chas}} “hour”, following the number rule: {{час|chas}} (one o'clock, with no number), {{два часа́|dva chasá}}, {{три часа́|tri chasá}}, {{пять часо́в|pyat' chasóv}}. Minutes are {{мину́ты|minúty}}: {{два часа́ два́дцать мину́т|dva chasá dvádtsat' minút}}, or simply {{два два́дцать|dva dvádtsat'}}.

**At what time?** {{в|v}} and the time: {{в два часа́|v dva chasá}} “at two”, {{в семь часо́в|v sem' chasóv}} “at seven”. You ask {{Во ско́лько?|Vo skól'ko?}} “At what time?”. To say which part of the day, add {{утра́|utrá}}, {{дня|dnya}} or {{ве́чера|véchera}}: {{в семь утра́|v sem' utrá}} “at 7 a.m.”, {{в семь ве́чера|v sem' véchera}} “at 7 p.m.”. Timetables use the 24-hour clock: {{в девятна́дцать часо́в|v devyatnádtsat' chasóv}}.

**On what day?** {{в|v}} and the day in the accusative (lesson 10), so only the days in {{-а|-a}} change: {{в сре́ду|v srédu}}, {{в пя́тницу|v pyátnitsu}}, {{в суббо́ту|v subbótu}}. Before {{вто́рник|vtórnik}}, {{в|v}} becomes {{во|vo}}, which is easier to say. Days are written with a small letter.

**Parts of the day** are single words with no preposition: {{у́тром|útrom}} “in the morning”, {{днём|dnyom}} “in the afternoon”, {{ве́чером|vécherom}} “in the evening”, {{но́чью|nóch'yu}} “at night”. With them: {{сего́дня|sevódnya}} “today”, {{за́втра|závtra}} “tomorrow”, {{вчера́|vcherá}} “yesterday”.

ex.tr: What time is it? — Two o'clock.
The class is at nine in the morning.

ex.t: Во ско́лько ты встаёшь? — В семь.
ex.r: Vo skól'ko ty vstayósh'? — V sem'.
ex.tr: What time do you get up? — At seven.

mistakes.why: On a day: {{в|v}} and the accusative, {{-а|-a}} → {{-у|-u}}.
After 5: {{часо́в|chasóv}}.
{{у́тром|útrom}} already means “in the morning”: no {{в|v}}.

practice.q: A friend invites you out. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Shall we go to the movies on Saturday?

practice.q: Your turn: say what you do on two days of the week, and at what time. Use {{в|v}} with a day and {{в|v}} with a time.

answers.t: В понеде́льник я рабо́таю, а в семь часо́в ве́чера у меня́ йо́га.
answers.r: V ponedél'nik ya rabótayu, a v sem' chasóv véchera u menyá yóga.
answers.tr: On Monday I work, and at seven in the evening I have yoga.

answers.t: В суббо́ту у́тром я гуля́ю в па́рке, а в воскресе́нье отдыха́ю до́ма.
answers.r: V subbótu útrom ya gulyáyu v párke, a v voskresén'ye otdykháyu dóma.
answers.tr: On Saturday morning I go for a walk in the park, and on Sunday I relax at home.

lessons.title: Say where you're going
lessons.summary: Say where you're going right now, on foot or by transport, and ask “Where to?”: “I'm going to the store, then to work.”
lessons.topic: {{идти́|idtí}} and {{е́хать|yékhat'}}; {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} with the accusative ({{куда́?|kudá?}}) or the prepositional ({{где?|gde?}}); {{домо́й|domóy}}

goal.t: Я иду́ в магази́н, а пото́м на рабо́ту.
goal.r: Ya idú v magazín, a potóm na rabótu.
goal.tr: I'm going to the store, and then to work.

dialog.t: А я иду́ на по́чту, пото́м в банк.
dialog.r: A ya idú na póchtu, potóm v bank.
dialog.tr: I'm going to the post office, then to the bank.
This evening we're going to the dacha.

blocks.p: **Two verbs for “go”.** Russian has no single verb for “go”. {{идти́|idtí}} is to go on foot; {{е́хать|yékhat'}} is to go by car, bus, train, anything with wheels. Both mean going somewhere right now, in one direction. (How to say you go somewhere often comes in a later lesson.)

**Where to?** In lesson 9, {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} with the prepositional said where something is ({{где?|gde?}}). When you're going there ({{куда́?|kudá?}} “where to?”), the same {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} take the **accusative**, just as in lesson 10: masculine and neuter places don't change, and {{-а|-a}} becomes {{-у|-u}}. A place that takes {{на|na}} for “where” takes it for “where to” too.

ex.tr: Where are you going? — To the airport.
Where are you off to? — To work.
ex.note: in quick speech the verb is often left out

mistakes.why: Going somewhere: {{в|v}} and the accusative. {{в магази́не|v magazíne}} is where you are.
Another city is too far to walk: by transport, {{е́хать|yékhat'}}.
“Home” is {{домо́й|domóy}} when you're going there, {{до́ма|dóma}} when you're there.

practice.q: You live in New York and you're going to Boston for the weekend. You say…
options: {{Я е́ду в Бо́стон.|Ya yédu v Bóston.}}
{{Я иду́ в Бо́стон.|Ya idú v Bóston.}}

practice.q: A neighbor stops you on the street. Choose your replies.

lines.why: Where to: the accusative, {{на по́чту|na póchtu}}.

lines.t: А где по́чта? Я не зна́ю.
lines.r: A gde póchta? Ya ne znáyu.
lines.tr: Where's the post office? I don't know.

lines.why: Where something is: the prepositional, {{на пло́щади|na plóshchadi}}, {{в це́нтре|v tséntre}}.

practice.tr: In the evening we're going home.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Where are you going?”
Your turn: where are you going today or tomorrow, and how? Use {{Я иду́…|Ya idú…}} or {{Я е́ду…|Ya yédu…}} with {{в|v}} or {{на|na}}.

answers.t: Сего́дня я иду́ в спортза́л, а за́втра е́ду на рабо́ту.
answers.r: Sevódnya ya idú v sportzál, a závtra yédu na rabótu.
answers.tr: Today I'm going to the gym, and tomorrow I'm going to work.

answers.t: Ве́чером я иду́ в кино́.
answers.r: Vécherom ya idú v kinó.
answers.tr: This evening I'm going to the movies.

lessons.title: Say what you can, may and must do
lessons.summary: Say what you can and can't do, ask permission, and say what you have to do: “Could you repeat that? I have to go.”
lessons.topic: {{мочь|moch'}} and {{уме́ть|umét'}}; {{мо́жно|mózhno}} and {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}}; {{мне на́до|mne nádo}}, {{мне ну́жно|mne núzhno}} + infinitive

goal.t: Извини́те, я не могу́. Мне на́до рабо́тать.
goal.r: Izviníte, ya ne mogú. Mne nádo rabótat'.
goal.tr: Sorry, I can't. I have to work.

dialog.tr: Shall we go to the movies tonight?

dialog.t: Сего́дня не могу́. Мне на́до рабо́тать.
dialog.r: Sevódnya ne mogú. Mne nádo rabótat'.
dialog.tr: I can't tonight. I have to work.

dialog.t: В семь. Ты мо́жешь купи́ть биле́ты?
dialog.r: V sem'. Ty mózhesh' kupít' biléty?
dialog.tr: At seven. Can you buy the tickets?

blocks.p: **Can.** {{мочь|moch'}} “to be able to, can” is followed by a verb in the infinitive: {{Я могу́ помо́чь.|Ya mogú pomóch'.}} “I can help.” Its forms are irregular:

**Know how to.** For a skill you've learned, Russian uses {{уме́ть|umét'}} (like {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}}: {{уме́ю|uméyu}}, {{уме́ешь|uméyesh'}}): {{Я уме́ю пла́вать.|Ya uméyu plávat'.}} “I can swim, I know how.” {{Я не могу́ пла́вать|Ya ne mogú plávat'}} says you aren't able to right now: maybe the water's too cold.

**May I? You can't.** {{мо́жно|mózhno}} “it's allowed, one may” and {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}} “it isn't allowed, one can't” need no person: {{Здесь мо́жно кури́ть?|Zdes' mózhno kurít'?}} “Can you smoke here?” — {{Нет, нельзя́.|Net, nel'zyá.}} {{Мо́жно?|Mózhno?}} on its own, at a door, means “May I come in?”.

**Have to.** {{на́до|nádo}} and {{ну́жно|núzhno}} (the same meaning) and an infinitive say what has to be done. Add who has to do it with the forms you know from saying your age: {{мне на́до|mne nádo}} “I have to”, {{тебе́ на́до|tebé nádo}} “you have to”, {{ему́ ну́жно|yemú núzhno}} “he needs to”…

ex.t: Я уме́ю гото́вить, но не уме́ю пла́вать.
ex.r: Ya uméyu gotóvit', no ne uméyu plávat'.
ex.tr: I can cook, but I can't swim.
They have to work on Saturday.

mistakes.why: After {{могу́|mogú}}: the infinitive.
Who has to: {{мне|mne}}, “to me”.

practice.q: A sign in a museum says {{Нельзя́ фотографи́ровать|Nel'zyá fotografírovat'}}. It means…

practice.why: A skill: {{уме́ть|umét'}}. {{Мне на́до пла́вать|Mne nádo plávat'}} is “I have to swim”.

practice.q: A friend wants to meet. Choose your replies.

options: Нет, в суббо́ту не могу́. Мне на́до рабо́тать.
Нет, в суббо́ту не мо́жет. Я на́до рабо́тать.
lines.why: “I can't”: {{не могу́|ne mogú}}; “I have to”: {{мне на́до|mne nádo}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you know how to do, and one thing you have to do this week.

answers.t: Я уме́ю игра́ть на гита́ре. В суббо́ту мне на́до рабо́тать.
answers.r: Ya uméyu igrát' na gitáre. V subbótu mne nádo rabótat'.
answers.tr: I can play the guitar. On Saturday I have to work.

answers.t: Я немно́го уме́ю гото́вить. Сего́дня мне ну́жно купи́ть хлеб.
answers.r: Ya nemnógo uméyu gotóvit'. Sevódnya mne núzhno kupít' khleb.
answers.tr: I can cook a little. Today I need to buy bread.

lessons.title: Say what you're going to do
lessons.summary: Talk about tomorrow, the weekend and the future: “Tomorrow I'll be working; on Sunday I'll relax.”
lessons.topic: The future with {{бу́ду|búdu}} + infinitive; {{бу́дет|búdet}} “there will be”

goal.t: За́втра я бу́ду рабо́тать, а в воскресе́нье бу́ду отдыха́ть.
goal.r: Závtra ya búdu rabótat', a v voskresén'ye búdu otdykhát'.
goal.tr: Tomorrow I'll be working, and on Sunday I'll relax.

dialog.t: Что ты бу́дешь де́лать в выходны́е?
dialog.r: Shto ty búdesh' délat' v vykhodnýye?
dialog.tr: What are you going to do on the weekend?

dialog.t: В суббо́ту я бу́ду убира́ть кварти́ру.
dialog.r: V subbótu ya búdu ubirát' kvartíru.
dialog.tr: On Saturday I'll be cleaning the apartment.

dialog.t: В воскресе́нье мы бу́дем гуля́ть в па́рке.
dialog.r: V voskresén'ye my búdem gulyát' v párke.
dialog.tr: On Sunday we'll go for a walk in the park.

blocks.p: The simplest future in Russian is a future form of {{быть|byt'}} “to be” and the infinitive: {{я бу́ду рабо́тать|ya búdu rabótat'}} “I'll work, I'll be working”, {{мы бу́дем отдыха́ть|my búdem otdykhát'}} “we'll relax”. Only {{бу́ду|búdu}} changes; the second verb stays as it is.

**Will be.** On its own, {{бу́ду|búdu}} means “I will be”: {{За́втра я бу́ду до́ма.|Závtra ya búdu dóma.}} “Tomorrow I'll be home.” {{бу́дет|búdet}} also means “there will be”: {{За́втра бу́дет дождь.|Závtra búdet dozhd'.}} “It's going to rain tomorrow.” And with {{у меня́|u menyá}}: {{У меня́ бу́дет вре́мя.|U menyá búdet vrémya.}} “I'll have time.”

**With which verbs?** All the verbs you know so far go with {{бу́ду|búdu}}: they're about activities that go on for a while or happen again and again (working, reading, waiting, relaxing). For one thing you'll get done (“I'll buy it”, “I'll call you”), Russian has another future, coming soon.

ex.t: Что ты бу́дешь пить? — Чай, пожа́луйста.
ex.r: Shto ty búdesh' pit'? — Chay, pozháluysta.
ex.tr: What will you have to drink? — Tea, please.

ex.t: За́втра я бу́ду до́ма весь день.
ex.r: Závtra ya búdu dóma ves' den'.
ex.tr: Tomorrow I'll be home all day.

ex.t: Ле́том мы бу́дем жить на да́че.
ex.r: Létom my búdem zhit' na dáche.
ex.tr: In summer we'll be living at the dacha.

ex.t: Я бу́ду ждать тебя́ в кафе́.
ex.r: Ya búdu zhdat' tebyá v kafé.
ex.tr: I'll wait for you at the café.

ex.t: В понеде́льник у меня́ бу́дет экза́мен.
ex.r: V ponedél'nik u menyá búdet ekzámen.
ex.tr: On Monday I'll have an exam.

mistakes.why: After {{бу́ду|búdu}}: the infinitive.
{{бу́ду|búdu}} already means “will be”.
{{бу́ду|búdu}} changes for the person: {{ты бу́дешь|ty búdesh'}}.

practice.tr: What are you going to do tomorrow?
I'll be waiting for you at home.

practice.q: You're a guest at a Russian home. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What will you have to drink?

lines.why: A short answer is enough. (After {{бу́ду|búdu}} would come the infinitive {{пить|pit'}}.)

lines.t: А что вы бу́дете де́лать за́втра?
lines.r: A shto vy búdete délat' závtra?
lines.tr: And what are you doing tomorrow?

practice.q: Your turn: what are you going to do on the weekend? Two things, with {{бу́ду|búdu}} and a verb.

answers.t: В суббо́ту я бу́ду убира́ть кварти́ру, а в воскресе́нье бу́ду смотре́ть фи́льмы.
answers.r: V subbótu ya búdu ubirát' kvartíru, a v voskresén'ye búdu smotrét' fíl'my.
answers.tr: On Saturday I'll be cleaning the apartment, and on Sunday I'll be watching movies.

answers.t: В выходны́е мы бу́дем отдыха́ть на да́че.
answers.r: V vykhodnýye my búdem otdykhát' na dáche.
answers.tr: On the weekend we'll be relaxing at the dacha.

lessons.title: Say what you've done and finished
lessons.summary: Say that something is done, read, bought or written, and not just that you were doing it: Russian's two kinds of verb.
lessons.topic: Aspect: imperfective and perfective verbs in the past ({{чита́л|chitál}} / {{прочита́л|prochitál}})

goal.t: Я уже́ прочита́л э́ту кни́гу.
goal.r: Ya uzhé prochitál étu knígu.
goal.tr: I've already read this book.

dialog.tr: I was doing it all evening!
Were doing it, or got it done?
And did you finish the book?
I read it! I read for two hours.

blocks.means: the way a verb looks at an action: as a process or a habit, or as one complete event with a result. Most Russian verbs come in pairs, one for each aspect.
the aspect of process and habit: {{чита́ть|chitát'}} “to read, to be reading”. All the verbs so far, except a few in fixed phrases, have been imperfective.
the aspect of one complete event with a result: {{прочита́ть|prochitát'}} “to read through, to finish reading”.

blocks.p: This is the heart of Russian verbs. English shows the difference with tenses (“I was reading”, “I've read it”); Russian uses two different verbs. The imperfective {{де́лал|délal}} says you were doing it, or did it, as an activity. The perfective {{сде́лал|sdélal}} says it got done: there's a result.

**How the pairs are made.** Often the perfective adds a prefix ({{с-|s-}}, {{про-|pro-}}, {{на-|na-}}, {{по-|po-}}): {{де́лать|délat'}} → {{сде́лать|sdélat'}}. Sometimes the middle of the verb changes ({{реша́ть|reshát'}} → {{реши́ть|reshít'}}), and a few pairs are different words ({{говори́ть|govorít'}} → {{сказа́ть|skazát'}}). Dictionaries give both.

**Which one?** Ask yourself: is this about the result, or about the activity? {{Я написа́л письмо́.|Ya napisál pis'mó.}} “I wrote the letter (it's written).” {{Я писа́л письмо́ весь ве́чер.|Ya pisál pis'mó ves' vécher.}} “I was writing the letter all evening.” Words like {{весь день|ves' den'}}, {{два часа́|dva chasá}}, {{ча́сто|chásto}} and {{всегда́|vsegdá}} go with the imperfective; {{уже́|uzhé}} “already” and {{наконе́ц|nakonéts}} “finally” usually with the perfective.

ex.tr: Yesterday we watched the new movie.
Have you decided yet? — Yes, I have.

ex.t: В де́тстве я ча́сто смотре́л мультфи́льмы.
ex.r: V détstve ya chásto smotrél mul'tfíl'my.
ex.tr: As a kid I often watched cartoons.

ex.t: Вчера́ я весь день писа́л отчёт и наконе́ц его́ написа́л.
ex.r: Vcherá ya ves' den' pisál otchót i nakonéts yevó napisál.
ex.tr: Yesterday I spent all day writing the report, and finally finished it.

mistakes.why: “All evening” is about the activity: the imperfective {{де́лал|délal}}.
“Finally” means it got done: the perfective.
“Every day” is a habit: the imperfective.

practice.t: Вчера́ я ___ письмо́ и отпра́вил его́.
practice.tr: Yesterday I wrote the letter and sent it.
practice.why: It got written (and then sent): the perfective.

practice.q: {{Я чита́л э́ту кни́гу|Ya chitál étu knígu}} tells you…
options: you spent time reading it (maybe not to the end)
practice.why: The imperfective is about the activity, not the result.

practice.q: You're a man, at work. Choose your replies.

options: Ещё нет. Я писа́л его́ весь день, но не написа́л.
Ещё нет. Я написа́л его́ весь день.
lines.why: All day: the activity, {{писа́л|pisál}}; not finished: {{не написа́л|ne napisál}}.

lines.t: А письмо́ клие́нту? Вы его́ отпра́вили?
lines.r: A pis'mó kliyéntu? Vy yevó otprávili?
lines.tr: And the letter to the client? Did you send it?

practice.tr: Yesterday we bought a new car.

practice.q: Say, as a woman: “I've already watched this movie.”
Your turn: say one thing you spent time doing yesterday (imperfective) and one thing you got done (perfective).

answers.t: Вчера́ я весь день рабо́тал, а ве́чером наконе́ц прочита́л кни́гу.
answers.r: Vcherá ya ves' den' rabótal, a vécherom nakonéts prochitál knígu.
answers.tr: Yesterday I worked all day, and in the evening I finally finished my book.

answers.t: Вчера́ я до́лго убира́ла кварти́ру, а пото́м купи́ла цветы́.
answers.r: Vcherá ya dólgo ubirála kvartíru, a potóm kupíla tsvetý.
answers.tr: Yesterday I spent a long time cleaning the apartment, and then I bought flowers.

lessons.title: Promise and offer to do things
lessons.summary: Promise, offer and say what you'll get done: “I'll call you tomorrow.” “I'll buy the bread.”
lessons.topic: The perfective future ({{позвоню́|pozvonyú}}, {{куплю́|kuplyú}}, {{сде́лаю|sdélayu}}) and {{бу́ду|búdu}} + imperfective

goal.t: Я тебе́ за́втра позвоню́.
goal.r: Ya tebé závtra pozvonyú.
goal.tr: I'll call you tomorrow.

dialog.t: Я куплю́. Я всё равно́ иду́ в магази́н.
dialog.r: Ya kuplyú. Ya vsyo ravnó idú v magazín.
dialog.tr: I'll buy some. I'm going to the store anyway.
Thanks! And will you make dinner?

dialog.t: Нет, у́жин пригото́вишь ты. А я помо́ю посу́ду.
dialog.r: Net, úzhin prigotóvish' ty. A ya pomóyu posúdu.
dialog.tr: No, you'll make dinner. And I'll wash the dishes.

blocks.p: Here's a surprise: perfective verbs have no present tense. When you put a perfective verb into the present forms, it means the **future**: {{я сде́лаю|ya sdélayu}} “I'll do it, I'll get it done”, {{я куплю́|ya kuplyú}} “I'll buy it”. It promises a result.

So there are two futures, chosen just as in the past: {{За́втра я бу́ду писа́ть отчёт.|Závtra ya búdu pisát' otchót.}} “Tomorrow I'll be working on the report.” {{За́втра я напишу́ отчёт.|Závtra ya napishú otchót.}} “Tomorrow I'll write the report (it'll be done).” Never put {{бу́ду|búdu}} before a perfective verb.

**Useful ones.** {{позвони́ть|pozvonít'}}: {{позвоню́|pozvonyú}}, {{позвони́шь|pozvonísh'}} “call”; {{купи́ть|kupít'}}: {{куплю́|kuplyú}}, {{ку́пишь|kúpish'}} “buy”; {{помо́чь|pomóch'}}: {{помогу́|pomogú}}, {{помо́жешь|pomózhesh'}} “help”; {{сказа́ть|skazát'}}: {{скажу́|skazhú}}, {{ска́жешь|skázhesh'}} “say, tell”; {{написа́ть|napisát'}}: {{напишу́|napishú}}, {{напи́шешь|napíshesh'}} “write”; {{прийти́|priytí}}: {{приду́|pridú}}, {{придёшь|pridyósh'}} “come”. Promises and offers are almost always made with verbs like these.

lessons.title: Ask someone to do something
lessons.summary: Ask, tell and invite: “Please speak more slowly.” “Come in, sit down!” “Let's go!”
lessons.topic: The imperative ({{-й|-y}}, {{-и|-i}}, {{-ь|-'}}, and {{-те|-te}} for {{вы|vy}}); aspect in requests; {{дава́й|daváy}}

goal.t: Говори́те, пожа́луйста, ме́дленнее.
goal.r: Govoríte, pozháluysta, médlenneye.
goal.tr: Please speak more slowly.

dialog.tr: Thank you. Here, this is for you.
Oh, thank you! Tea or coffee?
Delicious! Please give me the recipe!

blocks.means: the form of a verb for asking or telling someone to do something: Come in! Sit down!

blocks.p: **How to make it.** Take the {{они́|oní}} form, drop its ending, and add {{-й|-y}} after a vowel, {{-и|-i}} after a consonant (or {{-ь|-'}}, when the stress isn't on the ending). That's the form for {{ты|ty}}; for {{вы|vy}}, add {{-те|-te}}.

A few everyday ones are irregular: {{дать|dat'}} “give” → {{дай|day}}, {{да́йте|dáyte}}; {{есть|yest'}} “eat” → {{ешь|yesh'}}, {{е́шьте|yésh'te}}. And {{извини́те|izviníte}} “excuse me” is an imperative too: “excuse (me)”.

**Which aspect?** For one specific thing, the perfective: {{Скажи́те, пожа́луйста, где метро́?|Skazhíte, pozháluysta, gde metró?}} “Could you tell me where the subway is?”, {{Позвони́ мне!|Pozvoní mne!}} “Call me!”. The imperfective is for invitations and “go ahead”, and sounds warm, not pushy: {{Проходи́те!|Prokhodíte!}} “Come in!”, {{Сади́тесь!|Sadítes'!}} “Sit down!”, {{Бери́те!|Beríte!}} “Help yourself!”. With {{не|ne}}, use the imperfective: {{Не волну́йся!|Ne volnúysya!}} “Don't worry!”

**Let's.** {{Дава́й|Daváy}} (to a friend) or {{Дава́йте|Daváyte}} with the {{мы|my}} form of a perfective verb: {{Дава́й встре́тимся в суббо́ту.|Daváy vstrétimsya v subbótu.}} “Let's meet on Saturday.” Or with an imperfective infinitive: {{Дава́йте говори́ть по-ру́сски!|Daváyte govorít' po-rússki!}} “Let's speak Russian!”

ex.tr: Excuse me, where's the pharmacy around here?

ex.note: a warning about something that could happen by accident takes the perfective

lessons.title: Give, send and tell things to people
lessons.summary: Say who you give, send, write, tell and show things to: “I'm buying Mom a present.”
lessons.topic: The dative case ({{кому́?|komú?}}): {{-у|-u}}, {{-ю|-yu}}, {{-е|-e}}, {{-и|-i}}; {{мне|mne}}, {{тебе́|tebé}}, {{ему́|yemú}}…

goal.t: Я покупа́ю ма́ме пода́рок.
goal.r: Ya pokupáyu máme podárok.
goal.tr: I'm buying Mom a present.

dialog.tr: Yes. I'm looking for a present for my brother.

dialog.t: Отли́чно! А ещё я ищу́ что́-нибудь сестре́.
dialog.r: Otlíchno! A yeshchó ya ishchú shtó-nibud' sestré.
dialog.tr: Great! And I'm also looking for something for my sister.

blocks.means: the case of the person something is given, sent, told or shown to: {{Я пишу́ ма́ме.|Ya pishú máme.}} “I'm writing to Mom.” It answers {{кому́?|komú?}} “to whom?”.

blocks.p: You already know the dative from {{мне два́дцать лет|mne dvádtsat' let}} and {{мне на́до|mne nádo}}: “to me”. Now for nouns. English shows who gets something with “to” or with the word order (“I gave the book to Anna”, “I gave Anna the book”). Russian puts that person in the dative, with no preposition: {{Я дал А́нне кни́гу.|Ya dal Ánne knígu.}}

**Verbs that take the dative.** {{дать|dat'}} / {{дава́ть|davát'}} “give”, {{подари́ть|podarít'}} “give as a present”, {{купи́ть|kupít'}} “buy (for)”, {{писа́ть|pisát'}} “write”, {{сказа́ть|skazát'}} “tell”, {{показа́ть|pokazát'}} “show”, {{отпра́вить|otprávit'}} “send”. And two that surprise English speakers, because English uses no “to”: {{звони́ть|zvonít'}} “call (on the phone)” and {{помога́ть|pomogát'}} / {{помо́чь|pomóch'}} “help”: {{Я звоню́ ма́ме.|Ya zvonyú máme.}} {{Помоги́ мне!|Pomogí mne!}}

The pronouns are the ones you know from age: {{мне|mne}}, {{тебе́|tebé}}, {{ему́|yemú}}, {{ей|yey}}, {{нам|nam}}, {{вам|vam}}, {{им|im}}. And {{(Мо́жно) вам помо́чь?|(Mózhno) vam pomóch'?}} is what shop assistants say: “Can I help you?”.

ex.r: Shto ty podaríl zhené na den' rozhdéniya?

Could you show me this jacket, please?

mistakes.tr: I gave the book to Anna.

{{помо́чь|pomóch'}} takes the dative: {{мне|mne}}.

lessons.title: Say what you like, need and feel
lessons.summary: Say what you like, what you need and how you feel: “I like this city.” “I need a hat.” “I'm cold.”
lessons.topic: {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} and {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}}; {{ну́жен|núzhen}}, {{нужна́|nuzhná}}, {{ну́жно|núzhno}}, {{нужны́|nuzhný}}; {{мне хо́лодно|mne khólodno}}, {{мне ску́чно|mne skúshno}}

goal.t: Мне о́чень нра́вится э́тот го́род.
goal.r: Mne óchen' nrávitsa étot górod.
goal.tr: I really like this city.

dialog.t: Да, о́чень! Мне нра́вятся па́рки и метро́.
dialog.r: Da, óchen'! Mne nrávyatsa párki i metró.
dialog.tr: Yes, very much! I like the parks and the subway.
The weather, not so much. I'm cold!

dialog.t: Вам нужна́ ша́пка! Здесь ря́дом магази́н.
dialog.r: Vam nuzhná shápka! Zdes' ryádom magazín.
dialog.tr: You need a hat! There's a store nearby.
Thanks, I definitely need a hat.

blocks.p: **Like.** Russian turns “I like it” around: {{Мне нра́вится э́тот го́род.|Mne nrávitsa étot górod.}} is word for word “This city is pleasing to me”. The thing you like is the subject, in the nominative, and you are in the dative. So the verb agrees with the thing: {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} for one thing, {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}} for several.

table: {{Мне нра́вится э́тот го́род.|Mne nrávitsa étot górod.}}

blocks.p: **{{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} or {{люблю́|lyublyú}}?** {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} is for liking something, especially something new: a city, a dress, a movie. {{люблю́|lyublyú}} is stronger and lasts: things you love and always do. To say you liked something you saw or tried once, use the perfective past, which agrees with the thing: {{Мне понра́вился фильм.|Mne ponrávilsya fil'm.}} “I liked the movie.”, {{понра́вилась|ponrávilas'}} (feminine), {{понра́вилось|ponrávilos'}} (neuter), {{понра́вились|ponrávilis'}} (plural).

**Need.** {{Мне ну́жен…|Mne núzhen…}} “I need…” works the same way: the thing is the subject, and {{ну́жен|núzhen}} agrees with it: {{ну́жен|núzhen}}, {{нужна́|nuzhná}}, {{ну́жно|núzhno}}, {{нужны́|nuzhný}}. With a verb, it's {{ну́жно|núzhno}} or {{на́до|nádo}}, as you know: {{Мне ну́жно идти́.|Mne núzhno idtí.}}

**How you feel.** The same shape once more: the dative and a word in {{-о|-o}}. {{Мне хо́лодно.|Mne khólodno.}} “I'm cold.” {{Мне жа́рко.|Mne zhárko.}} “I'm hot.” {{Мне ску́чно.|Mne skúshno.}} “I'm bored.” {{Мне интере́сно.|Mne interésno.}} “I'm interested.” {{Мне пло́хо.|Mne plókho.}} “I feel sick.” {{Мне ве́село.|Mne véselo.}} “I'm having fun.”

mistakes.why: The thing you like is the subject; you are in the dative: {{мне|mne}}.
Several things: {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}}.
{{ну́жен|núzhen}} agrees with the thing: {{ша́пка|shápka}} is feminine, so {{нужна́|nuzhná}}.

practice.why: How you feel: {{мне|mne}} and {{хо́лодно|khólodno}}. {{Я холо́дный|Ya kholódnyy}} would mean you're a cold person!

lessons.title: Say what something is about
lessons.summary: Say what a book or a movie is about, what you're thinking about, and who you're talking about.
lessons.topic: {{о|o}} + the prepositional; {{обо мне|obo mne}}, {{о нём|o nyom}}, {{о ней|o ney}}; adjectives in {{-ом|-om}}, {{-ой|-oy}}

goal.t: Э́то фильм о любви́.
goal.r: Éto fil'm o lyubví.
goal.tr: It's a movie about love.

dialog.tr: About a big family in Moscow.

dialog.t: Интере́сно. А о ком ты сейча́с ду́маешь? Ты тако́й гру́стный.
dialog.r: Interésno. A o kom ty seychás dúmayesh'? Ty takóy grústnyy.
dialog.tr: Interesting. And who are you thinking about? You look so sad.

dialog.t: О сестре́. Она́ сейча́с в больни́це.
dialog.r: O sestré. Oná seychás v bol'nítse.
dialog.tr: My sister. She's in the hospital.
Oh no… Tell me about her.

blocks.p: {{о|o}} “about” takes the prepositional, the case of {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} for “where” (lesson 9), with the same endings. {{О чём?|O chom?}} “About what?” and {{О ком?|O kom?}} “About whom?” ask about it. Before a vowel, {{о|o}} becomes {{об|ob}}: {{об э́том|ob étom}} “about this”, {{об А́нне|ob Ánne}}.

**Adjectives in the prepositional** end in {{-ом|-om}} (masculine and neuter) or {{-ой|-oy}} (feminine): {{в большо́м до́ме|v bol'shóm dóme}} “in a big house”, {{о но́вой рабо́те|o nóvoy rabóte}} “about the new job”, {{в ру́сском рестора́не|v rússkom restoráne}}. After {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}}, {{щ|shch}}, when the ending isn't stressed, they are {{-ем|-em}} and {{-ей|-ey}}: {{о хоро́шем фи́льме|o khoróshem fíl'me}}, {{о хоро́шей пого́де|o khoróshey pogóde}}.

**Verbs.** {{говори́ть о|govorít' o}} “talk about”, {{ду́мать о|dúmat' o}} “think about”, {{расска́зывать|rasskázyvat'}} / {{рассказа́ть о|rasskazát' o}} “tell about”, {{мечта́ть о|mechtát' o}} “dream of”, {{знать о|znat' o}} “know about”. And to say what something is about: {{кни́га о…|kníga o…}}, {{фильм о…|fil'm o…}}, {{пе́сня о…|pésnya o…}}. Watch out for {{любо́вь|lyubóv'}} “love”: {{о любви́|o lyubví}}.

ex.tr: He dreams of a big car.
What do you know about this?

mistakes.why: {{о|o}} takes the prepositional: {{о любви́|o lyubví}}.
After {{о|o}}: {{нём|nyom}}, {{ней|ney}}, {{них|nikh}}.
“About what?” is {{О чём?|O chom?}}

practice.why: A feminine adjective in the prepositional: {{-ой|-oy}}.

lessons.title: Say who you're with
lessons.summary: Say who you live, go and talk with, and what your coffee comes with: “My sister and I are going to the movies.”
lessons.topic: The instrumental case with {{с|s}}: {{-ом|-om}}, {{-ем|-em}}, {{-ой|-oy}}, {{-ей|-ey}}, {{-ью|-'yu}}; {{со мной|so mnoy}}, {{с ним|s nim}}…; {{мы с дру́гом|my s drúgom}}

goal.t: Я иду́ в кино́ с подру́гой. Хо́чешь с на́ми?
goal.r: Ya idú v kinó s podrúgoy. Khóchesh' s námi?
goal.tr: I'm going to the movies with a friend. Want to come with us?

dialog.tr: No, with my sister. And you?

dialog.t: Я живу́ с дру́гом. Мы с ним вме́сте рабо́таем.
dialog.r: Ya zhivú s drúgom. My s nim vméste rabótayem.
dialog.tr: I live with a friend. He and I work together.

dialog.t: В суббо́ту мы с сестро́й идём в кино́. Хоти́те с на́ми?
dialog.r: V subbótu my s sestróy idyóm v kinó. Khotíte s námi?
dialog.tr: On Saturday my sister and I are going to the movies. Do you two want to come with us?

blocks.means: the case for “with” (who you're with, what something comes with), for the tool you do something with, and for what someone works as or becomes. It answers {{с кем?|s kem?}} “with whom?” and {{чем?|chem?}} “with what?”.

blocks.p: {{с|s}} “with” takes the **instrumental**, your fifth case. Masculine and neuter words end in {{-ом|-om}}, feminine words in {{-ой|-oy}}:

table: {{с бра́том|s brátom}}, {{с молоко́м|s molokóm}}, {{с учи́телем|s uchítelem}}

blocks.p: After {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}}, {{щ|shch}} and {{ц|ts}}, an unstressed {{-ом|-om}} or {{-ой|-oy}} is written {{-ем|-em}} or {{-ей|-ey}}: {{с му́жем|s múzhem}}, {{с Ма́шей|s Máshey}}. Adjectives end in {{-ым|-ym}} (masculine) and {{-ой|-oy}} (feminine): {{с но́вым дру́гом|s nóvym drúgom}}, {{с ру́сской подру́гой|s rússkoy podrúgoy}}.

**My friend and I.** Russian says “we with my friend”: {{мы с дру́гом|my s drúgom}} “my friend and I”, {{мы с ней|my s ney}} “she and I”, with the verb in the {{мы|my}} form. And “with” for food and drink: {{чай с лимо́ном|chay s limónom}}, {{ко́фе с молоко́м|kófe s molokóm}}, {{пирожо́к с мя́сом|pirozhók s myásom}}.

ex.t: С кем ты живёшь? — С му́жем.
ex.r: S kem ty zhivyósh'? — S múzhem.
ex.tr: Who do you live with? — With my husband.

lessons.title: Talk about your job and your hobbies
lessons.summary: Say what you work as, what you wanted to be, and what you do in your free time: “I work as a teacher, and I do yoga.”
lessons.topic: The instrumental without {{с|s}}: {{рабо́тать врачо́м|rabótat' vrachóm}}; {{быть|byt'}} and {{стать|stat'}} + instrumental; {{занима́ться спо́ртом|zanimátsa spórtom}}

goal.t: Я рабо́таю программи́стом, а в свобо́дное вре́мя занима́юсь му́зыкой.
goal.r: Ya rabótayu programmístom, a v svobódnoye vrémya zanimáyus' múzykoy.

dialog.t: Я врач. Но в де́тстве я хоте́ла стать актри́сой!

blocks.p: The instrumental has a second big job: saying what someone **works as or becomes**. {{Кем вы рабо́таете?|Kem vy rabótayete?}}, word for word “As whom do you work?”, means “What do you do for a living?”. The answer is in the instrumental, with no word for “as”: {{Я рабо́таю врачо́м.|Ya rabótayu vrachóm.}} “I work as a doctor.”

**Be and become.** In the present there's no “is”, so the nominative: {{Я врач.|Ya vrach.}} But after the past, the future and the infinitive of {{быть|byt'}}, and always after {{стать|stat'}} “to become”, the job or role goes into the instrumental: {{Он был учи́телем.|On byl uchítelem.}} “He was a teacher.” {{Я хочу́ стать врачо́м.|Ya khochú stat' vrachóm.}} “I want to become a doctor.”

table: {{Она́ хоте́ла стать актри́сой.|Oná khotéla stat' aktrísoy.}}

blocks.p: **Hobbies.** {{занима́ться|zanimátsa}} and the instrumental means “to do, to go in for” a sport, a hobby or a subject: {{занима́ться спо́ртом|zanimátsa spórtom}}, {{му́зыкой|múzykoy}}, {{йо́гой|yógoy}}, {{ру́сским языко́м|rússkim yazykóm}}. It has {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}}'s forms with {{-ся|-sya}} on the end: {{я занима́юсь|ya zanimáyus'}}, {{ты занима́ешься|ty zanimáyesh'sya}}, {{он занима́ется|on zanimáyetsa}} (lesson 33 explains {{-ся|-sya}}). {{интересова́ться|interesovátsa}} “to be interested in” works the same way: {{я интересу́юсь исто́рией|ya interesúyus' istóriyey}}. And {{Чем ты занима́ешься?|Chem ty zanimáyesh'sya?}} asks “What do you do?”.

ex.tr: What do you want to be? — An engineer.
My father worked as a driver.

ex.t: Я занима́юсь спо́ртом три ра́за в неде́лю.
ex.r: Ya zanimáyus' spórtom tri ráza v nedélyu.
ex.tr: I work out three times a week.

ex.r: Chem ty zanimáyesh'sya v svobódnoye vrémya?

ex.r: V détstve ya byl óchen' tíkhim rebyónkom.
